prompt: You are designing a multi-agent system in Microsoft Foundry for a consumer-loan origination workflow. The pipeline must triage the application, extract data from uploaded documents, compute a credit decision, and run a regulatory compliance check before a loan offer is generated. Requirements: end-to-end latency under 12 seconds, token cost minimized, every decision auditable, and the compliance step must be able to reject and loop the application back to extraction with a reason. A prototype using one generalist agent with every tool registered is inconsistent and frequently calls the wrong tool. Which design meets ALL requirements?
options: An orchestrator-subagent pattern where a lightweight orchestrator routes each stage to a narrow specialist agent (triage, extraction, decision, compliance) that owns only its own tools, with the compliance agent able to raise a revision event that the orchestrator sends back to extraction.
A single generalist agent with a very long system prompt that lists every lending rule and tool so it can complete all stages in one pass.
A peer-to-peer mesh where all four specialist agents broadcast to each other simultaneously and the first complete decision is accepted.
A parallel fan-out where all four stages run at once and the orchestrator merges whichever results arrive first.
explanation: The orchestrator-subagent pattern decomposes the goal into narrow, auditable stages, controls token cost by giving each subagent only its own context and tools, and supports the required compliance loop-back through an explicit revision path. A single generalist with a giant prompt inflates cost and does not fix wrong-tool reliability; a peer-to-peer mesh and unconditional parallel fan-out break the strict stage dependencies, cannot support the loop-back, and waste tokens by running every stage for every application.

prompt: You are architecting a procurement multi-agent system. A purchase request must be validated, matched against budget, then sent for a human manager's approval when it exceeds $10,000, and finally dispatched to the ERP. Compliance requires a tamper-evident record of who approved, what amount, and when, and rejected requests must return to the validator with the manager's note. Which orchestration pattern and gating strategy satisfy ALL constraints?
options: Parallel fan-out where validation, budget-matching, and manager approval run simultaneously and are merged.
A sequential orchestrator with explicit human-in-the-loop approval only for amounts over the threshold, durable audit records at each gate, and a rejection loop-back to the validator.
A peer-to-peer design where the validator and dispatcher message the manager directly and the manager's chat reply is the approval record.
A hub-and-spoke where the hub auto-approves requests under a daily aggregate cap to avoid interrupting the manager.
explanation: The workflow has strict sequential dependencies, a conditional human approval gate, an audit requirement, and a rejection loop-back. A sequential orchestrator that gates each stage, records approvals durably, and loops rejections back satisfies all of these. Parallel fan-out breaks the validation-to-approval dependency; peer-to-peer with a chat reply is not a tamper-evident audit record; a daily aggregate cap is not per-request human approval and would violate the compliance rule.

prompt: An enterprise is standardizing its agent platform. Two needs must be met: (1) individual agents built with different frameworks must discover each other's capabilities and delegate tasks using a common protocol without a central broker; and (2) each agent must connect to third-party tool servers and data sources using a vendor-neutral client-server standard. A reviewer warns that conflating the two protocols would force a design where either agents cannot delegate peer-to-peer or tool access is locked to one runtime. Which combination should you standardize on?
options: Use A2A for both tool access and agent delegation, since A2A also carries tool schemas.
Use MCP for both tool access and agent delegation, since MCP is the broader standard.
Use MCP for tools, data, and tool servers, and A2A for cross-framework agent delegation and capability discovery.
Use a custom REST API for both concerns to avoid protocol dependency.
explanation: MCP standardizes client-server access to tools, resources, and tool servers, while A2A standardizes peer-to-peer agent delegation and capability discovery across frameworks. They solve different problems; using one for both conflates distinct concerns (MCP is not a peer agent-delegation standard and A2A is not a tool/data access standard). A custom REST API reintroduces coupling and maintenance cost.

docs.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Azure AI Foundry

prompt: You are defining identities for a healthcare multi-agent system with a scheduling agent and a billing agent coordinated by a supervisor agent. A security review requires least privilege, per-agent attribution in audit logs, and the smallest possible blast radius if any one agent is compromised. The supervisor must be able to trigger scheduling and billing but must never itself read clinical notes or issue invoices. Which identity and permission design is correct?
options: Grant all three agents one shared service principal with combined scheduling and billing permissions so delegation never fails.
Give the supervisor the union of both tool sets so it can act as a fallback if a specialist is down.
Allow the supervisor to impersonate either specialist on demand so it can call tools directly while keeping two identities.

Give each specialist its own scoped managed identity with only its own tools, and give the supervisor its own identity with delegation-only permissions and no direct access to scheduling, billing, or clinical data.
explanation: Least privilege and minimized blast radius require per-agent scoped identities, with the supervisor delegated permissions rather than accumulated or impersonated rights. A shared identity breaks attribution and widens blast radius; a union toolset on the supervisor violates the explicit restriction on reading clinical notes or issuing invoices; impersonation muddies attribution and expands the supervisor's effective access.

prompt: You are designing a research assistant that works across many sessions on a 300-page technical specification. Users report that, deep into a session, the agent forgets constraints stated in the first message and re-cites passages it already concluded were irrelevant. You must retain the user's standing constraints and the agent's prior conclusions across turns and sessions without exceeding the model's context window. What is the correct memory design?
options: Persist standing constraints and resolved conclusions to long-term memory (for example a vector store) and retrieve the relevant slices each turn, keeping only the current working excerpts in context.
Use a sliding window that keeps only the last 10 turns plus a one-line summary, discarding the original constraint text.
Increase max_tokens to the model maximum so the full document and full transcript always fit.
Re-send the entire 300-page document and full transcript every turn to prevent any loss.
explanation: Moving durable facts (constraints, conclusions) to long-term memory and retrieving the relevant slices each turn solves both sliding-window amnesia and summary drift while staying within the context window. A sliding window drops the early constraints; raising max_tokens does not overcome a finite window for a 300-page document plus a long transcript; resending everything overflows the window and inflates cost.

prompt: A customer-support multi-agent system has a triage agent that is drifting: it sometimes answers billing questions instead of only classifying and routing, and it invents refund amounts. You must reduce hallucination and tool misuse at the source while keeping operational cost low. The triage agent currently has access to a refund tool and a knowledge search tool. Which change is most effective and least expensive?
options: Add a second validator agent that fact-checks every triage answer after the fact and corrects invented refunds.
Redefine the persona with a narrow role and explicit do/don't boundaries, remove the refund and search tools from its toolset, and constrain its output to a structured classification only.
Add a longer system prompt listing every possible billing question and the exact refund amount to state for each.
Increase the model temperature so the agent stays on generic, safe responses.
explanation: Tightening the persona (narrow role plus explicit boundaries), removing unnecessary tools, and constraining the output to a structured classification directly reduces drift and hallucination at the source at minimal cost. A downstream validator is reactive and expensive and does not prevent misuse; a longer prompt cannot enumerate every question and encourages answering; higher temperature increases randomness and hallucination.

prompt: You are designing the retrieval layer of a multi-agent RAG system over dense regulatory contracts. A single obligation often spans several paragraphs, but your fixed 500-token chunks with small overlap return fragmented passages and the answer agent misreads obligations. You must improve retrieval precision while controlling embedding and storage cost. Which chunking and retrieval approach should you use?
options: Increase every chunk to 8,000 tokens so each obligation is guaranteed to be whole.
Use maximum overlap (50% of every chunk) so boundaries are always covered.
Chunk by semantic boundaries (sections or clauses) with parent-document references and retrieve the parent section when a child chunk matches.
Skip chunking and embed each entire contract as a single document.
explanation: Semantic chunking with parent-document (small-to-big) retrieval keeps obligations coherent for the answer agent while embedding focused chunks for precision, controlling both embedding and storage cost. Oversized chunks dilute embedding quality; maximum overlap is redundant and costly; whole-document embeddings destroy precision and return entire contracts into the context.

prompt: You are choosing an orchestration topology for an incident-response multi-agent system. Three specialist agents (detection, remediation, reporting) must share findings dynamically, and any agent may need to query any other agent's results during an investigation. You must avoid a single point of failure and keep latency low, but you also need a clear, auditable record of who communicated with whom. Which topology best fits, and why?
options: Hub-and-spoke, so a central orchestrator can throttle and log all messages and never fails.
Sequential pipeline, so detection always feeds remediation which feeds reporting in a fixed order.
Parallel fan-out, so all three agents run at once and never need to talk to each other.
Peer-to-peer, with each agent able to message the others directly, plus distributed tracing to reconstruct the communication graph for audit.
explanation: Peer-to-peer supports the dynamic, many-to-many sharing and low-latency direct queries the scenario requires, and distributed tracing supplies the auditable record. Hub-and-spoke introduces a single point of failure and a bottleneck; a sequential pipeline imposes a fixed order that does not match dynamic investigations; parallel fan-out forbids the inter-agent queries that are explicitly required.

prompt: You are applying Zero Trust to a multi-agent system where a coordinator agent fans out to retrieval, code-generation, and deployment subagents. Security requires that a compromised retrieval agent cannot reach the deployment tooling, and a compromised coordinator cannot silently execute a deployment. Each subagent must authenticate to its own resources, and lateral movement between subagents must be blocked. Which combination of controls is the strongest and most operationally sound?
options: Give each agent its own managed identity scoped to least-privilege RBAC on only its resources, enforce network segmentation so agents cannot reach each other's endpoints, and require an explicit approval gate before any deployment action.
Use one admin-level API key shared by all agents, and rely on the coordinator's prompt to prevent cross-agent calls.
Use per-agent API keys but allow full network connectivity between agents to keep latency low.
Give only the coordinator a real identity and let subagents inherit its permissions when invoked.
explanation: Zero Trust requires per-agent identity, least-privilege RBAC, network segmentation to block lateral movement, and a human approval gate for high-impact actions. A shared admin key, full network connectivity, and inherited permissions all widen blast radius and enable lateral movement or silent execution, violating the stated requirements.

docs.label: Enterprise security for Azure AI Foundry

prompt: You are developing an agent in Azure AI Foundry Agent Service that must answer questions about internal HR policies stored in SharePoint and must always cite the current version when a policy changes. Requirements: minimize latency for common questions and never return stale policy content. Which tool integration and caching strategy should you implement?
options: Copy the policy documents into the agent's system prompt daily so the model always has the text.
Register SharePoint as a grounded data source and disable caching for policy lookups so each answer is grounded in live data, while caching the stable system prompt.
Use a single API key for SharePoint and hardcode the policy text into the agent code.
Register SharePoint as a runtime tool and enable semantic caching keyed on the exact user question to minimize latency.
explanation: Grounding via a data source retrieves the current policy at query time, and disabling cache for policy content preserves freshness; caching the stable system prompt still saves cost. Prompt-embedded and hardcoded text go stale and inflate prompt size; a shared API key is a management and security risk; semantic caching keyed on the question can serve outdated answers when policies change.

docs.label: Azure AI Foundry Agent Service tools

prompt: Two teams are selecting agent frameworks. Team A needs explicit, programmable control flow, plugins, and deep enterprise integration with Azure and .NET. Team B needs autonomous agent-to-agent conversation with group chat to solve tasks dynamically. Both teams must deploy on Azure AI Foundry. Which framework assignment is correct?
options: AutoGen for Team A and Semantic Kernel for Team B.
Both teams on AutoGen, since it also supports plugins and .NET.
Semantic Kernel for Team A and AutoGen for Team B.
Both teams on Semantic Kernel, since its group chat feature equals AutoGen's.
explanation: Semantic Kernel emphasizes explicit orchestration, plugins, and .NET/Azure integration, matching Team A; AutoGen emphasizes multi-agent conversation and group chat, matching Team B. Swapping them or forcing both teams onto one framework misaligns with the stated needs and forfeits each framework's strengths.

prompt: You are building an agent that can submit purchase orders. It must obtain explicit human approval for any order over $5,000, the approval must be auditable (who, when, and what), and the approval process must not interrupt the agent's progress on orders under $5,000. Which implementation satisfies ALL constraints?
options: Pause the agent and prompt the same user inline for every order, using the chat message as the approval record.
Execute all orders immediately and email the user afterward to retroactively approve the large ones.
Allow the agent full autonomy but cap its total daily spend at $5,000.
Implement a conditional human-in-the-loop gate that triggers only for orders over $5,000, routing to an approval queue with a durable record (user, timestamp, amount) before execution.
explanation: A conditional approval gate satisfies all constraints: explicit approval only when the threshold is exceeded, a durable and auditable record, and no interruption for small orders. Inline prompts interrupt every order and a chat message is not a robust audit record; retroactive email is not preventive; a daily spend cap is not per-order human approval.

prompt: Your multi-agent system re-sends a large stable system prompt and a set of few-shot examples with every request, and a separate high-volume FAQ agent receives many near-duplicate user questions. You must reduce both cost and latency without losing answer quality. Which caching strategy combination is most appropriate?
options: Enable prompt caching for the stable system prompt and few-shot examples, and enable semantic caching for the FAQ agent's near-duplicate questions.
Use semantic caching for the system prompt and prompt caching for the FAQ questions.
Use exact-match response caching for both, keyed only on the literal user string.
Disable caching and shorten the system prompt to reduce cost.
explanation: Prompt caching stores and reuses the stable prefix (system prompt and few-shot examples); semantic caching matches near-duplicate questions by meaning. Semantic caching does not apply to a system prompt, and exact-match response caching misses near-duplicates; disabling caching forgoes the available savings.

prompt: A customer-service agent handles sessions with 100+ turns. Its context manager summarizes every 10 turns into a rolling summary and discards older turns. QA reports that late in the session the summary has drifted: the customer's account number and a prior refund agreement are mis-stated or lost, causing wrong actions. What is the best fix?
options: Replace rolling summaries with a pure sliding window of the last 10 turns only.
Keep a hierarchical memory: store immutable facts (account number, agreements) separately from the running narrative summary and re-inject the verified facts each turn.
Summarize less often (every 30 turns) so early facts survive longer.
Increase temperature so the summarizer paraphrases more faithfully.
explanation: Summary drift is mitigated by separating durable, immutable facts from the evolving narrative and re-injecting them, rather than folding everything into a lossy rolling summary. A pure sliding window loses early facts entirely (sliding-window amnesia); less-frequent summaries only delay drift while increasing token usage; higher temperature increases hallucination and drift.

prompt: You are hardening an agent that can query a SQL database and email customers. A red-team exercise showed a crafted prompt made the agent run a destructive UPDATE and then email a forged message to a customer. You must place guardrails at the correct layers to prevent both the destructive action and the forged outbound message. Which set of controls is correct?
options: Input guardrail only: run every user prompt through a prompt shield before it reaches the agent.
Output guardrail only: filter the email content before sending.
Input prompt shield, a tool-call policy (deny or allowlist that blocks destructive SQL unless pre-approved), and an output content filter before external send.
Tool-call guardrail only: restrict SQL to SELECT statements.
explanation: Defense in depth requires guarding all three surfaces: inputs (prompt shield against injection), tool calls (a policy or allowlist that blocks destructive actions), and outputs (content filter before external send). A single-layer control leaves the other attack surfaces exposed; a tool-only SELECT restriction does not stop injection or forged email content, and input-only or output-only controls are incomplete.

prompt: You are implementing the retrieval layer of a multi-agent RAG app on Azure AI Search. The corpus mixes technical manuals and FAQs. Hybrid search returns good recall but poor precision: the answer agent receives many irrelevant chunks and wastes tokens. You need higher precision without sacrificing recall. What should you do?
options: Switch to keyword-only search to make results exact.
Increase top-k to return more chunks so the correct one is guaranteed to be present.
Keep hybrid search and add a reranker (for example the semantic ranker) to reorder and trim to top-k, plus a minimum relevance threshold to drop weak matches.
Embed chunks at whole-document granularity to reduce the number of chunks.
explanation: Hybrid retrieval plus a semantic reranker and a relevance threshold improves precision (fewer, higher-quality chunks) while preserving the recall provided by hybrid search. Keyword-only search loses semantic recall for paraphrased queries; a larger top-k worsens precision and token cost; coarser chunks reduce precision and inflate each returned result.

prompt: You are adding long-term memory to an agent so it can recall facts about a user across separate sessions. Requirements: the memory must be queryable by meaning, updates must not require re-embedding the entire store, and stale or incorrect facts must be removable individually. Which implementation is most appropriate?
options: Use a vector database for embeddings with metadata (user id, timestamp) and support upsert and delete by id so facts can be added, updated, and expired.
Store all facts as one JSON blob appended to the system prompt each session.
Store facts in a key-value cache keyed by the exact user's last question.
Fine-tune the model on each user's facts.
explanation: A vector store provides semantic recall plus per-item metadata and upsert/delete for incremental updates and expiry. A system-prompt JSON blob does not scale, is not queryable by meaning, and cannot be selectively removed; a key-value cache is exact-match only; fine-tuning is expensive, per-user unscalable, and bakes stale facts into weights.

prompt: You are developing an agent that must decompose a complex report request into independent subtasks (gather sales data, fetch inventory, compute a forecast) and then combine the results into one answer. The subtasks have no dependencies on each other, and you need the lowest possible end-to-end latency. Which orchestration pattern should you use?
options: Peer-to-peer, where each agent waits for another agent to ask it to start.
Parallel fan-out (hub-and-spoke), where a coordinator dispatches the three independent subtasks concurrently and aggregates their results.
Sequential pipeline, where sales, inventory, and forecast run one after another.
Single agent that performs the three tasks in a loop until done.
explanation: Parallel fan-out runs independent subtasks concurrently and aggregates results, minimizing end-to-end latency. Peer-to-peer does not provide a natural aggregation point and adds hand-off latency; a sequential pipeline serializes independent work and is slower; a single-agent loop is sequential and slower still.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: You are using an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate agent answer quality against a rubric. You find the judge gives inflated scores because it tends to agree with well-formatted answers even when they are factually wrong. You must make the evaluation reliable and cost-effective. What should you do?
options: Use a single zero-shot prompt asking the judge to rate each answer from 1 to 5.
Replace the judge with a human for every evaluation to remove bias.
Increase the judge model's temperature to make its scores more varied.
Calibrate the judge against a human-labeled golden set, use the same rubric, add grounding or reference context, periodically sample human agreement, and test for position bias.
explanation: Reliable LLM-as-a-judge requires calibration to human labels, a consistent rubric, grounding context, ongoing agreement sampling, and bias mitigation (including position bias). A bare zero-shot 1-5 score is uncalibrated and prone to inflation; full human review is not cost-effective or scalable; higher temperature adds randomness, not accuracy.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: You are evaluating a multi-agent RAG system where the answer agent sometimes produces fluent but unsupported answers (citations do not back the claim) and sometimes returns correct but off-topic answers. You must select the metric pair that catches BOTH failure modes. Which pair should you use?
options: Fluency and coherence only.
Latency and cost per token.
Retrieval hit rate only.
Groundedness and relevance.
explanation: Groundedness evaluates whether claims are supported by the grounding content, catching unsupported answers; relevance evaluates whether the answer addresses the query, catching off-topic answers. Fluency and coherence measure style and would score fluent unsupported answers well; latency and cost are operational metrics; retrieval hit rate is a proxy that does not measure answer quality.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Your production multi-agent system occasionally produces wrong answers, but you cannot tell whether the fault is in the retrieval step, a subagent's reasoning, or the final synthesis. You must diagnose the root cause across the agent chain with minimal added code. What should you implement?
options: Enable end-to-end distributed tracing (for example Azure AI Foundry tracing) that captures each agent's inputs, outputs, and tool calls as spans, correlated by run or session.
Add print statements in each agent's code and parse the logs manually.
Log only the final answer and the user query to a table.
Re-run the failing query against a single-agent baseline only.
explanation: Distributed tracing with spans per agent and tool gives per-stage visibility and correlation, enabling root-cause isolation across the chain. Manual print statements are unstructured and fragile; logging only the final answer gives no intermediate visibility; a single-agent baseline cannot pinpoint which stage in the chain failed.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: You are asked to reduce token cost in a multi-agent system. Telemetry shows the largest cost driver is a coordinator agent that re-reads a 40 KB system prompt and a 60 KB tool-results payload every turn, across 10 subagents. You must reduce cost without changing the agents' capabilities. What should you do FIRST?
options: Switch to a cheaper model for all agents.
Trim the system prompt, use prompt caching for the stable prefix, and summarize or compress tool results before passing them to subagents.
Reduce the number of subagents from 10 to 5.
Increase the model's max_tokens so fewer turns are needed.
explanation: The first, capability-preserving step targets the actual cost driver: shrink the prompt, cache the stable prefix, and compress tool outputs. Switching to a cheaper model risks quality; cutting subagents changes architecture and capabilities; raising max_tokens increases cost and does not reduce input tokens.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Before promoting a new multi-agent version to production, you must decide what evaluation evidence to collect under a limited budget and time. Which evaluation plan gives the strongest signal about BOTH correctness and safety with the least wasted effort?
options: Evaluate only on synthetic single-turn prompts generated randomly.
Deploy to production immediately and monitor user feedback for the first week.
Evaluate only on a public benchmark unrelated to your domain.

Build a golden dataset of representative multi-turn scenarios with expected outcomes, run offline metrics (groundedness, relevance), run a targeted AI red-team pass on safety, and compare against the current version.
explanation: A representative golden set plus offline quality metrics plus targeted red-teaming plus version comparison provides both correctness and safety signal efficiently. Random synthetic prompts, unrelated public benchmarks, and production-only monitoring are unrepresentative or unsafe and waste effort.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Your orchestrator fans out a question to eight independent subagents and waits for all to return before synthesizing. Measured P95 latency is nine seconds, driven by the single slowest subagent; token cost is also high because the slow agent is retried. You need to cut latency without losing answer quality. What should you do?
options: Wait for only the first subagent to return and use that answer.
Run the eight subagents sequentially to smooth latency.
Increase the straggler's max_tokens so it finishes thinking.
Set a per-agent timeout and continue with the responses received (partial fan-out) instead of retrying the straggler, while caching or shortening the straggler's path.
explanation: The long tail is the straggler; a timeout plus proceed-with-received (with graceful degradation) and optimizing the slow path cuts P95 latency without blocking on all subagents. First-to-return-only loses information and lowers quality; sequential execution increases total latency; more tokens increase latency, not reduce it.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Six months after launch, users report your agent's answers have subtly declined in quality, but no code changed. You suspect data drift (source documents changed) and prompt or model drift. You need an ongoing, automated way to detect regression. What should you implement?
options: A continuous evaluation pipeline that periodically runs a fixed golden dataset through the agent and alerts when metrics (groundedness, relevance) fall below a threshold, plus telemetry on document index freshness.
A one-time manual review of a sample of answers.
Rebuild the index every night and assume quality is fine.
Ask users to flag bad answers manually.
explanation: Continuous evaluation against a stable golden set with threshold alerting detects regression from data, prompt, or model drift, and index freshness telemetry flags stale grounding data. A one-time manual review is point-in-time; nightly rebuilds do not detect answer-quality drift; user flagging is reactive and incomplete.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: You are running LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and suspect the judge is biased toward whichever candidate answer appears first in the comparison, and that it occasionally rubber-stamps fluent-but-wrong answers. You must detect and mitigate these biases before relying on the judge for promotion decisions. Which action set is most appropriate?
options: Trust the judge's raw scores and promote the highest-scoring answer immediately.
Randomize answer order across evaluation runs and compute agreement against a human-labeled golden set, then treat low-agreement categories as needing human review.
Use a stronger judge model and assume stronger models have no biases.
Drop the rubric and let the judge score on overall impression.
explanation: Position bias is detected by randomizing answer order across runs, and calibration is measured by agreement against a human-labeled golden set; categories with low agreement should be escalated to humans. Trusting raw scores ignores known bias; a stronger model still exhibits position and formatting bias; removing the rubric increases inconsistency and bias.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Your multi-agent RAG system scores well on groundedness but QA finds the answer agent still often fails to use the single most relevant retrieved passage, instead citing a tangentially related one. You need a metric that specifically measures whether the retrieval step surfaced the correct context, so you can fix the retrieval layer rather than the answer layer. Which metric should you focus on?
options: Fluency of the final answer.
End-to-end latency.
Retrieval precision and recall (for example whether the correct passage is retrieved and ranked near the top).
Cost per token of the answer agent.
explanation: Retrieval precision and recall isolate the retrieval layer, measuring whether the correct context was surfaced and ranked well, which is exactly the failure mode described. Fluency, latency, and cost are downstream or operational metrics that do not reveal whether retrieval returned the right passage.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: Your multi-agent system serves two enterprise tenants, and each agent calls a shared CRM tool. A security review flags the risk that a compromised agent could read another tenant's records. You must prevent cross-tenant data access with minimal operational overhead. What should you implement?
options: One shared API key for all agents, with the CRM's own login handling tenant scoping.
Network-layer isolation only (separate subnets per tenant) with no per-agent identity.
Log and monitor all agent access without changing access control.
Per-agent scoped identities (for example managed identities) with tenant-isolated credentials and RBAC so each agent can access only its tenant's records.
explanation: Zero Trust requires per-agent, scoped identities with tenant-isolated credentials and least-privilege RBAC to prevent lateral movement and enforce cross-tenant isolation. A shared API key and network-only isolation do not enforce data-level authorization, and monitoring-only detects rather than prevents cross-tenant access.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: An agent must call a downstream API (Microsoft Graph) to read the signed-in user's calendar. Security requires that the agent act only with the user's delegated permissions and never hold a long-lived shared secret. Which authentication approach should you use?
options: OAuth 2.0 on-behalf-of (OBO) flow, where the user's token is exchanged for a downstream token with delegated permissions, using the agent's managed identity where possible.
A single service principal with application permissions and a client secret stored in the agent config.
Embed a user's personal API key in the agent and call the API directly.
Basic authentication with a hardcoded username and password.
explanation: The on-behalf-of flow propagates the signed-in user's identity and delegated permissions to downstream APIs without storing user credentials or long-lived app secrets. Application permissions with a client secret, embedded personal API keys, and hardcoded basic credentials all violate the delegated-permission and secret-hygiene requirements.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: You must assess whether your customer-facing multi-agent system can be manipulated to exfiltrate internal documents via a chain of agent hand-offs. Which approach is most appropriate and proportionate?
options: Only test each agent in isolation with benign prompts.
Automated prompt-injection fuzzing plus targeted, human-led adversarial testing of the multi-agent hand-off chain, documented and remediated before release.
Skip adversarial testing because the model is a trusted vendor model.
Run a single static code review of the prompts.
explanation: AI Red Teaming combines automated adversarial fuzzing with human-led, scenario-based testing, including multi-agent chaining, to find cross-agent prompt-injection and exfiltration paths. Isolation-only benign testing, skipping testing, and a static prompt review all miss runtime cross-agent attacks.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: You are releasing a new version of a multi-agent orchestrator. You need to validate the new version on real traffic with instant rollback, but you also want to avoid a bad version affecting 100% of users at once. Which deployment strategy should you use?
options: Big-bang cutover to the new version at a fixed time.
Blue/green with both environments fully deployed but routing 100% of traffic to green immediately.
Canary deployment: route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, monitor metrics, gradually increase, with automated rollback on regression.
Shadow deployment that mirrors traffic to the new version but never serves it.
explanation: Canary deployment offers gradual real-traffic exposure with monitoring and rollback, avoiding a 100% blast radius while still serving real traffic. Blue/green's instant full cutover affects all users at once; big-bang is all-at-once; shadow deployment never serves real traffic and therefore does not validate end-to-end serving.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: A regulated enterprise is deploying a multi-agent system where one agent drafts customer communications. Compliance requires that outputs never contain personally identifying information (PII) or prohibited financial claims, and every generated communication must be attributable to the responsible agent for audit. What should you implement?
options: Rely on prompt instructions telling the agent not to include PII.
Only log outputs after sending, for later audit.
Encrypt the output channel end-to-end.
Apply an output content filter and PII detection plus a prohibited-claims check at the output layer, block or redact before send, and emit per-agent audit logs with the responsible agent's identity.
explanation: Enforcement (content filter, PII detection, and prohibited-claims checks with block or redact) at the output layer plus per-agent attribution satisfies the compliance controls. Prompt-only instructions are soft and unenforced; post-send logging does not prevent prohibited content from being sent; encryption does not filter PII or prohibited claims within the message.

docs.label: Responsible AI in Azure AI Foundry

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: Your team manually edits prompts and agent tool definitions directly in production, which has caused several outages. You want to introduce CI/CD so every change to prompts, tools, or agent definitions is versioned, tested, and promoted through development, test, acceptance, and production (DTAP). Which practice should you adopt?
options: Treat prompts and agent/tool definitions as code in source control, run automated evaluation and regression tests in CI, and promote through DTAP environments with gated deployments.
Continue manual edits but add a change-request form.
Version only the model weights and keep prompts in a shared document.
Freeze all prompts and definitions so no changes are ever needed.
explanation: Treating prompts and agent/tool definitions as versioned code with automated evaluation gates and gated DTAP promotion gives reproducibility and safe rollout. Manual edits with a form are still manual and unversioned; versioning only weights leaves prompts unversioned and drifting; freezing everything blocks necessary improvement.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: Two regulated tenants (Bank A and Bank B) use your multi-agent platform. Their compliance rules require that no network traffic, model deployments, or data can be shared between tenants, and the platform must remain manageable. What isolation architecture should you use?
options: One shared model deployment and shared agents, but with per-tenant prompt prefixes.
Fully separate deployments, managed network isolation, and per-tenant resources and credentials so tenants share no data plane, model endpoints, or network.
A single virtual network for both tenants with per-tenant network security groups.
One shared vector index with tenant-id metadata filters.
explanation: Regulated isolation requires complete separation of the data plane, model endpoints, network, and credentials per tenant. Shared deployments, a shared virtual network, and a shared vector index all introduce co-mingling risk even with prompt prefixes, network security groups, or metadata filters.

docs.label: Enterprise security for Azure AI Foundry

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: An attacker embeds instructions inside a document that your document-processing agent ingests, causing a downstream action agent to exfiltrate data. You must reduce the risk of such indirect prompt injection propagating across agents. Which combination is most effective?
options: Trust all ingested documents and rely on the model to ignore malicious text.
Only apply a content filter to the final output, not the input.
Treat retrieved document content as untrusted data, delimit and clearly separate it from instructions, apply prompt shields, and constrain the action agent's tool permissions so it cannot exfiltrate.
Give the action agent full tool access but log everything.
explanation: Indirect prompt injection is mitigated by clearly delimiting and separating untrusted data from instructions, applying prompt shields, and enforcing least-privilege tool scoping so even a manipulated agent cannot exfiltrate. Trusting documents, output-only filtering, and logging-with-full-access do not prevent the attack.
